paper_title: FlashMask-3: Efficient and Expressive Mask-Aware Distributed Attention

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Long-context training of large language and multimodal models couples structured attention masks (document, prefix-LM, share-question, sliding-window, block-sparse) with multi-node context parallelism, making the mask a dominant bottleneck. FlashMask's column-wise sparse mask compresses them from $O(n^2)$ to $O(n)$ via four query-axis boundary vectors, covering broad structured patterns. Implemented for Ampere GPUs, it neither exploits FlashAttention-3's TMA/WGMMA warp-specialized pipeline on Hopper nor supports distribution. The column-wise sparse mask is indexed by key positions but stores query-axis interval boundaries. Under any multi-chunk context-parallel assignment, it reduces per-rank mask localization to a provably zero-communication \emph{clip--shift--max} on the boundary vectors, compatible with the single-GPU kernel. FlashMask-3 introduces a mask-aware Hopper kernel with three-role warp specialization atop FlashAttention-3's TMA/WGMMA pipeline, plus a mask-aware distributed extension: zero-communication mask localization, a sparsity-aware load balancer (HCC-IPO), and a mask-aware compute-communication overlap with mask-driven communication pruning, whose forward all-gather uses topology-aware hierarchical routing. On a single H100 across 12 masks at 4K--128K context, it improves achieved TFLOPs over FlashMask, FlexAttention, and MagiAttention by 45--141%, 34--71%, and 2--44%. At context-parallel degrees 4--32 with 8K sequence per device, it attains 31--75% compute-communication overlap efficiency and improves throughput over Megatron-Core CP ring, Megatron-Core CP all-gather, and MagiAttention by $1.80\times$--$3.71\times$, $1.71\times$--$2.92\times$, and $1.09\times$--$1.46\times$. In end-to-end training of a 118B-A14B MoE at 128K on 128 H100 GPUs, it raises throughput by 7.3--11.0% over a Dual Chunk all-gather baseline, with attention forward+backward 24.5--44.9% faster.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Long-context training of large language and multimodal models increasingly relies on structured attention masks, including document masks [Dao et al., 2022], prefix-LM masks [Wang et al., 2026], share-question masks [Deng et al., 2025], sliding-window masks [Beltagy et al., 2020], and blocksparse patterns [Child et al., 2019, Yuan et al., 2025, Lu et al., 2025], to encode training-data semantics Equal contribution. Corresponding author. 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). within single packed batch. As context grows toward hundreds of thousands of tokens and training scales to multi-node context parallelism [Liu et al., 2023, Jacobs et al., 2023, Narayanan et al., 2021], masks become first-class bottleneck: mask materialization, mask-aware kernel scheduling, and mask-induced load imbalance [Jiang et al., 2025, Tao and Huang, 2025] come to dominate step time. Programmable attention compilers [He et al., 2024] handle arbitrary masks but trail FlashAttention3 (FA3) [Shah et al., 2024] in Hopper throughput; FA3 itself first-classes only causal, full, and varlen-document masks. The column-wise sparse representation of FlashMask [Wang et al., 2024] fills the expressiveness gap by encoding masks through four O(n) boundary vectors, covering 12+ structured patterns within an exact tiled kernel [Dao et al., 2022, Dao, 2023]. However, FlashMask was implemented on Ampere GPUs and predates FA3: it exploits neither Hoppers TMA/WGMMA warp-specialized pipeline [Shah et al., 2024] nor any form of distributed context parallelism [Liu et al., 2023, Brandon et al., 2023, Narayanan et al., 2021]. We observe structural property that resolves the distributed gap. Because the column-wise sparse mask is indexed by key positions but stores query-axis intervals [Wang et al., 2024], per-rank mask localization under any multi-chunk CP assignment reduces to an elementwise clipshiftmax on the boundary vectors, requiring no cross-rank communication and producing rank-local tensor directly compatible with the single-GPU kernel (Theorem 1). Building on this property, we present FlashMask-3,3 which organizes mask-awareness along two axes: (i) mask-aware Hopper kernel with three-role warp specialization integrating column-wise sparse scanning into the FA3 TMA/WGMMA pipeline (3.1); and (ii) mask-aware distributed extension combining zero-communication mask localization (3.2), sparsity-aware hierarchical load balancer(3.3), and mask-aware computecommunication overlap [Chang et al., 2024, NVIDIA, 2023] with topology-aware hierarchical routing and mask-driven communication pruning (3.4). Our main contributions are as follows: Mask-aware Hopper kernel. three-role warp specialization (KV Index Generator, KV Loader, MMA Consumer) integrates column-wise sparse mask processing into the asynchronous TMA/WGMMA pipeline at near-zero overhead, complemented by preemptive persistent-tile scheduler that restores SM-level balance under irregular masks. Mask-aware distributed extension. zero-communication clipshiftmax mask localization with provable correctness; sparsity-aware hierarchical load balancer (HCC-IPO); and mask-aware compute-communication overlap with mask-driven communication pruning, whose forward all-gather uses topology-aware hierarchical routing and whose backward reduce-scatter is overlapped with attention recomputation through bitmask-AMO (Atomic Memory Operations) synchronization. Empirical evaluation. On single H100 GPU across 12 structured masks at context lengths from 4K to 128K, FlashMask-3 improves achieved TFLOPs over FlashMask, FlexAttention, and MagiAttention by 45% to 141%, 34% to 71%, and 2% to 44%, respectively. Under context-parallel degrees from 4 to 32 with 8K sequence per device, it attains 31% to 75% compute-communication overlap efficiency and improves throughput over Megatron-Core CP (ring), Megatron-Core CP (all-gather) and MagiAttention by 1.80 to 3.71, 1.71 to 2.92 and 1.09 to 1.46 respectively. In end-to-end training of 118B-A14B MoE model at 128K context on 128 H100 GPUs (CP degree 16), our distributed extension raises the training throughput by 7.3% to 11.0% over the same system using Dual Chunk balancing and all-gather communication.

sections.title: 2 Background
sections.content: 2.1 FlashAttention-3 on Hopper GPUs The FlashAttention family [Dao et al., 2022, Rabe and Staats, 2021, Milakov and Gimelshein, 2018, Dao, 2023] computes exact attention = softmax(QK / d)V without materializing the score matrix, through tiling and online softmax. FlashAttention-3 [Shah et al., 2024] targets Hopper GPUs by adding asynchronous TMA loads, WGMMA instructions, and warp-specialized producer consumer pipelines: producer warp group issues TMA loads while consumer warp groups execute WGMMA, coordinated through small set of cross-warp barriers. FlashMask-3 builds on this 3The name aligns with FlashAttention-3, on which our Hopper kernel is built, mirroring how FlashMask [Wang et al., 2024] built on FlashAttention-2 [Dao, 2023]. asynchronous backbone, inserting mask processing as an additional warp-specialized stage rather than inline branches in the main compute loop (3.1). 2.2 Column-wise sparse mask representation FlashMask [Wang et al., 2024] encodes structured attention masks from the perspective of key tokens. The score matrix is split along the diagonal into lower-triangular and upper-triangular regions, and the mask at each key is encoded by four boundary vectors LTS, LTE, UTS, UTE Zn 0, with the masked query rows at key given by [LTSj, LTEj) [UTSj, UTEj). The tensor is indexed by key positions but stores query-axis values, structural asymmetry that we exploit for zero-communication distributed mask localization in 3.2. Inside tiled kernel, blockwise max/min along the key axis classifies each querykey tile as fully-masked, partially-masked, or unmasked, supporting tile skipping (3.1) and the cost model in 3.3. Two alternative routes target masks beyond the FlashAttention-native subset. FlexAttention [He et al., 2024] JIT-compiles an arbitrary user-defined mask_mod function via Triton-based DSL [Tillet et al., 2019]; the compiled kernel handles arbitrary mask logic but follows code path separate from FA3 and incurs per-mask compilation cost. MagiAttention [Tao and Huang, 2025] introduces an AttnSlice formulation paired with dedicated Flex-Flash-Attention (FFA) kernel that natively supports arbitrary mask types; its distributed extension materializes per-rank mask structure via slice-cutting operations. In contrast, FlashMask-3 retains the O(n) column-wise sparse representation and reduces per-rank mask localization to clipshiftmax on the boundary vectors at zero cross-rank communication (3.2), with no per-rank slice materialization or kernel recompilation. 2.3 Context parallelism and load balancing Context parallelism (CP) shards the query sequence across ranks; each rank computes attention for its local queries against the global K, stream exchanged across ranks. Ring Attention [Liu et al., 2023] circulates K, around device ring overlapped with blockwise attention; Striped Attention [Brandon et al., 2023] interleaves tokens for causal-load balance; DeepSpeed Ulysses [Jacobs et al., 2023] converts sequence parallelism into head parallelism via all-to-all; Megatron CP [Narayanan et al., 2021] pairs early and late query chunks (dual chunking) for balanced causal workload and obtains global K, through forward all-gather and backward reduce-scatter. Under expressive masks, the monotonic-load assumption underlying dual chunking breaks, coupling two further challenges: balancing mask-induced sparse compute across ranks, and overlapping forward all-gather and backward reduce-scatter with mask-aware computation, both addressed in 3. 2.4 Computecommunication overlap Computecommunication overlap operates at two levels. At the kernel-stream level, FLUX [Chang et al., 2024] fuses all-gather and reduce-scatter into GEMM tiles via signal-based dependencies, achieving near-complete overlap for linear layers; Ring Attention [Liu et al., 2023] overlaps K, circulation with blockwise attention via dual CUDA streams. Extending tile-level fusion to attention is non-trivial because online softmax requires per-tile rescaling that degrades throughput upon splitting. At the topology level, NVSHMEM [NVIDIA, 2023] exposes GPU-initiated one-sided put/get over symmetric memory, enabling fine-grained overlap without CPU staging. These mechanisms form the substrate on which 3.4 builds mask-aware overlap that prunes communication of fully-masked KV chunks and tracks per-segment readiness via bitmask-AMO synchronization. comprehensive discussion of additional related work is provided in Appendix B.

sections.content: FlashMask-3 takes column-wise sparse mask alongside (Q, K, ) tensors, with the same mask schema and the same kernel binary serving both single-GPU and query-sharded context-parallel execution. Mask-awareness propagates through four layers of the execution stack via four cooperating mechanisms (3.13.4), all reusing the same full/partial/unmasked block classification off the column-wise sparse boundary vectors at kernel runtime, host-side preprocessing, and communicationside filtering. Figure 1 summarizes the cooperation. 3 Figure 1: Overview of FlashMask-3 across four layers of the execution stack. Figure 2: Three-role warp specialization in the FlashMask-3 Hopper kernel: KV Index Generator (mask scan), KV Loader (TMA load), and MMA Consumer (WGMMA score), connected by three asynchronous pipelines. 3.1 Hopper-optimized mask-aware kernel On Hopper, FA3 overlaps TMA-issued KV loads with WGMMA score and online softmax via two warp-group roles [Shah et al., 2024]; inserting column-wise sparse mask scanning into either role would stall the TMA queue or introduce barrier inside the WGMMA critical path. We observe that FA3s Producer warp group dedicates 128 threads to TMA issue while single thread suffices to launch each op, leaving 96 threads idle every iteration; FlashMask-3 reclaims these threads as third warp-specialized role, the KV Index Generator, which scans the column-wise sparse boundaries described in 2.2 and emits queue of valid blocks classified as fully-masked, partially-masked, or unmasked via the blockwise max/min of {LTS, LTE, UTS, UTE}. The KV Loader consumes the queue and issues TMA loads only for listed blocks; the MMA Consumer runs the WGMMA score path, applying row-interval mask only on partially-masked blocks (Figure 2). The same classification feeds host-side preprocessing in 3.3 and communication-side filtering in 3.4 on independent code paths. Beyond warp specialization, irregular masks make per-Q-block valid-K-block counts vary by an order of magnitude, leaving SMs that own long-tail Q-blocks straggling under static tile-to-SM dispatch. sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: In this section, we evaluate FlashMask-3 through comprehensive set of experiments designed to assess single-GPU kernel efficiency (4.1), distributed scalability (4.2), and end-to-end training throughput on production-scale MoE workload (4.3), followed by component-level ablations (4.4). All experiments are conducted on machines equipped with NVIDIA H100 80GB SXM5 GPUs interconnected via NVLink within each node and RoCE across nodes, with 8 GPUs per node and Intel Xeon Platinum 8468V CPUs (48 cores). We use CUDA 12.4, CUTLASS (commit afa177) [Thakkar et al., 2023] and NVSHMEM 3.2.5 throughout. Baseline configurations are as follows: MagiAttention (commit d97b72), FlexAttention (PyTorch 2.8.0), and Megatron 2.8.0. Unless otherwise stated, all experiments use head dimension of = 128 and the BF16 data type. Detailed experimental configurations are provided in Appendix D.1.1. Speed measurements are repeated; error bars in the figures and values in the tables denote 1 standard deviation. 4.1 Single-GPU Kernel Performance We first isolate the kernel-level performance of FlashMask-3 by benchmarking on single H100 GPU against FlashMask, FlexAttention, and MagiAttention. We sweep sequence lengths from 4K to 128K across 12 representative sparse mask patterns (see Equation 5 and Figure 5). The data construction method and experiment settings follows that described in Section A.5.2 [Wang et al., 2024]. Across this entire grid, FlashMask-3 improves achieved TFLOPs/s over FlashMask, FlexAttention, and MagiAttention by 45%141%, 34%71%, and 2%44%, respectively, outperforming all three 7 Figure 5: Kernel FWD & BWD throughput (TFLOPs/s) on single H100 GPU. (5) The 82.6% mean speedup over FlashMask validates the combined effect of our three-role warpspecialized pipeline, asynchronous TMA prefetching, Ping-Pong scheduling, and the PPT scheduler on Hopper. Against FlexAttention, the 55.3% mean gain reflects the overhead of runtime mask evaluation via torch.compile and the absence of Hopper-native execution pipeline. FlashMask-3 also surpasses MagiAttention by 15.0% in geometric mean (excluding the Random Eviction mask, on which MagiAttentions block-sparse representation is ill-suited, resulting in over 50 slowdown). Even on patterns favorable to block-sparse encoding, FlashMask-3 remains competitive or superior, demonstrating that the column-wise sparse representation achieves broad expressiveness without sacrificing efficiency. Across all comparisons, the speedup increases monotonically with sequence length (e.g., +66.2% +97.3% over FlashMask from 8K to 128K), confirming that our architectural optimizations yield compounding benefits as attention becomes increasingly memory-bound. Detailed per-mask TFLOPs/s results are provided in Appendix D.1.3. 4.2 Context Parallelism Scalability To evaluate the scalability of FlashMask-3 under context parallelism (CP), we compare against two representative baselines, namely Megatron-Core CP (both its ring and all-gather variants) and MagiAttention, on three practically relevant mask patterns: Causal Document Mask, Document Mask, and Prefix LM Document Mask. At CP degrees 4 and 8, all communication is confined to intra-node NVLink interconnects, whereas scaling to CP 16 and 32 introduces inter-node traffic. Despite this transition, FlashMask-3 sustains strong scaling efficiency. On the Causal Document Mask, its throughput increases from 430.5 TFLOPs/s at CP = 4 to 471.8, 491.8, and 501.6 TFLOPs/s at CP = 8, 16, and 32, respectively. Across all supported mask patterns and CP degrees, FlashMask-3 achieves 1.09 to 1.46 higher throughput than MagiAttention, outperforms Megatron-Core CP (all-gather) by 1.71 to 2.92, and surpasses Megatron-Core CP (ring) by 1.80 to 3.71. 4.3 End-to-End Training Throughput The preceding sections measure attention in isolation; we now report throughput for full training steps. We train 118B-A14B MoE model at 128K context on 128 H100 GPUs (16 nodes) with CP degree 16, per-device local sequence length of Slocal=8K tokens, Hq=64 query heads, Hkv=8 KV heads, and document mask. The baseline is FlashMask-3 with Dual Chunk balancing and all-gather communication, i.e. with the balancer of 3.3 and the overlap of 3.4 disabled. Because the share of step time spent in attention depends on mask sparsity, we repeat the comparison on three datasets with average mask sparsity 70%, 80%, and 86%. Table 1 reports gains of 7.3% / 7.7% / 11.0% in end-to-end throughput with both components enabled, at 70% / 80% / 86% sparsity, against attention forward+backward speedups of 24.5% / 42.1% / 44.9% (at 70% sparsity, 10900.5 ms per step down to 8757.6 ms). The end-to-end gain is smaller because attention accounts for only 43.5% / 25.8% / 24.4% of forward+backward compute time in the full configuration, and the end-to-end measurement also covers gradient synchronization and the optimizer update, which our method does not modify. Each component helps on its own, contributing 2.8% / 4.4% / 5.7% (balancing) and 5.4% / 4.2% / 5.9% (overlap), and chunk-skip pruning is worth further 2.0% / 2.9% / 1.5%. Hierarchical routing is required for the two to compose at this cross-node scale: with it disabled, balancing plus overlap falls to 1.7% / 1.5% / +1.9%, below overlap alone, because the balancer spreads chunks across nodes and that traffic is no longer confined to congruence groups (3.4). The default of 4 backward pipeline stages follows the rule of 3.4 at =16: halving it to 2 costs up to 3.6%, while raising it to 8 yields no significant further gain. FlashMask-3 computes exact attention: mask localization matches the global mask (Theorem 1), and the balancer, overlap, and pruning change only how work is placed, not what is computed. Convergence and downstream quality are therefore unaffected; Appendix D.3 compares the loss of an otherwise identical run without context parallelism. 4.4 Ablation Study Complementing the end-to-end breakdown of 4.3, we conduct three groups of ablation experiments that isolate each key component proposed in FlashMask-3 across mask patterns, sequence lengths, 9 (a) (b) Figure 7: (a) Speedup of the Preemptive Persistent Tile (PPT) scheduler over the static scheduler across different mask patterns and sequence lengths on single H100 GPU. Effect of Preemptive Persistent Tile (PPT). We compare three tile-scheduling strategies on single H100 GPU: (i) static scheduler that assigns fixed tile grid, (ii) single-tile scheduler that dispatches one work tile at time, and (iii) the proposed PPT scheduler. As shown in Figure 7(a), across 12 mask configurations at sequence lengths of 8K, 32K, and 128K, PPT consistently outperforms the static scheduler by up to 12%, demonstrating that preemptive, persistent tile execution effectively amortizes scheduling overhead and improves streaming multiprocessor (SM) utilization. Effect of load balancing. We compare four workload partitioning strategies under CP: (i) naïve baseline that evenly splits the KV sequence, (ii) Dual Chunk, (iii) Longest-Processing-Time first (LPT) [Graham, 1969], and (iv) our proposed Iterative Pairwise Optimization (IPO). We report the peak-to-average ratio of per-device computation time, where value closer to 1.0 indicates more balanced distribution. As shown in Figure 8, FlashMask-3 attains an overlap efficiency ranging from 0.31 to 0.75, validating the effectiveness of our mask-aware hierarchical compute-communication.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: FlashMask-3 establishes that the column-wise sparse mask representation, originally single-GPU memory optimization, also serves as the right interface for distributing expressive masks at zero communication on Hopper-class hardware. The method preserves one column-wise sparse mask abstraction and one FA3-derived kernel across single-GPU and multi-node settings, with maskawareness propagated through Hopper kernel scheduling, hierarchical load balancing, and computecommunication overlap. Empirical evaluation across 12 structured masks at context lengths up to 128K on single H100 GPU and context parallelism up to =32 yields consistent improvements in single-GPU TFLOPs, compute-communication overlap, and distributed throughput over representative single-GPU and distributed mask baselines. On end-to-end training of 118B-A14B MoE model at 128K context across 128 H100 GPUs, these mechanisms yield 7.3%11.0% throughput gain.

sections.title: A Limitations and Broader Impact
sections.content: Limitations. The method covers the column-wise sparse mask family of Wang et al. [2024]; masks whose per-column masked rows do not decompose into two intervals require representation extensions. The Hopper kernel exploits TMA/WGMMA and assumes Hopper-class architectures; porting to other architectures requires re-targeting the warp specialization. The hierarchical overlap of 3.4 assumes per-node 8-GPU NVLink islands with same-rank IB topology; clusters with different topologies need different inter-node mapping. Hierarchical routing is currently applied only to the all-gather 12 operation; extending it to the backward reduce-scatter is left as future work. Empirical claims rely on production-scale long-context settings; smaller contexts may not amortize the scheduler overhead. Finally, our benchmarks cover representative but not exhaustive set of QKV tensor configurations; systematic sweep over batch sizes and query/key-value head ratios beyond those reported in 4.2 and 4.3 is left to future work. Broader impact. By improving the throughput and energy efficiency of long-context training, FlashMask-3 lowers the cost barrier for academic and open-source long-context multimodal research and reduces the carbon footprint of large-scale training. The same efficiency gains can also lower the cost of training capability-amplifying models, which is an externality common to research on large-scale training infrastructure.

sections.title: B Extended Related Work
sections.content: IO-aware exact attention. FlashAttention [Dao et al., 2022] introduced tiling and online softmax [Milakov and Gimelshein, 2018, Rabe and Staats, 2021] to compute exact attention in O(N ) memory without materializing the score matrix. FlashAttention-2 [Dao, 2023] swapped the loop order and optimized warp-level work partitioning, reaching 5073% of A100 peak throughput. FlashAttention-3 [Shah et al., 2024] further added Hopper-native TMA/WGMMA pipelining and FP8 support, achieving 740 TFLOPs/s on H100. Block-Sparse FlashAttention [Dao et al., 2022] augments the tiled kernel with an O(N 2/B2) binary block mask for tile skipping; FlashMasks column-wise sparse representation achieves O(N ) storage with token-level granularity. Compiler-driven attention. FlexAttention [He et al., 2024] JIT-compiles arbitrary mask_mod functions into Triton [Tillet et al., 2019] kernels, offering maximal flexibility at the cost of per-mask compilation overhead and code path separate from FA3s Hopper-native pipeline. Under distributed CP, each rank independently reconstructs the local block mask at O(QK/B2) cost. FlashMask-3 avoids both issues through fixed kernel binary and zero-communication mask localization. Learnable block-sparse attention. NSA [Yuan et al., 2025] combines compression, top-k block selection, and sliding-window branches in an end-to-end differentiable architecture that is hardwarealigned and natively trainable from pretraining. MoBA [Lu et al., 2025] routes each query to its top-k KV blocks via MoE-style gating, enabling seamless switching with full attention. Both learn which tokens to attend to and require architectural modification. FlashMask-3 solves complementary problem: efficiently computing pre-specified structural mask with no model changes required. Structured mask representations. MagiAttention [Tao and Huang, 2025] represents masks as AttnSlice triples (Qrange, Krange, MaskType), cut along Q/K axes for distribution; this requires dedicated FFA kernel with per-slice atomics. FlashMask [Wang et al., 2024] uses column-wise sparse boundary vectors at O(N ) storage, covering 12+ structured mask patterns. FlashMask-3 extends this to distributed settings through an elementwise clipshiftmax transform that preserves the single-GPU kernel interface at zero cross-rank communication. Context parallelism. Ring Attention [Liu et al., 2023] circulates KV on device ring with dualstream overlap, achieving 50% GPU utilization under causal masks due to inherent load imbalance [Li et al., 2023]. Striped Attention [Brandon et al., 2023] restores causal balance via round-robin token assignment (1.451.65 over Ring) but supports only causal masks. DeepSpeed Ulysses [Jacobs et al., 2023] converts to head parallelism via all-to-all, natively supporting arbitrary masks but requiring Nheads mod = 0. USP [Fang and Zhao, 2024] unifies Ulysses (intra-node) with Ring (inter-node). Megatron CP [Narayanan et al., 2021] employs dual chunking for causal balance; under irregular masks such as shared-question (RLHF) or multi-document masks, its linear-cost assumption fails and per-rank utilization degrades significantly. Load balancing under irregular masks. DCP [Jiang et al., 2025] (SOSP 2025) models CP scheduling as hypergraph partitioning over block-level workloads, achieving <5% imbalance at the cost of heavyweight solver. MagiAttention [Tao and Huang, 2025] uses chunk-level LPT-greedy assignment [Graham, 1969] based on AttnSlice areas. FlashMask-3 derives per-chunk valid-block counts directly from the column-wise boundary vectors and solves the scheduling subproblem with provable optimality guarantees (3.3), avoiding external solver overhead. 13 Computecommunication overlap. Ring Attention [Liu et al., 2023] relies on dual CUDA streams, which suffer SM contention when large attention kernels starve communication of resources. FLUX [Chang et al., 2024] demonstrates that kernel-level tile fusion eliminates this contention for GEMMs, but online softmax prevents straightforward extension to attention. MagiAttention uses DeepEP-based [Zhao et al., 2025] GroupCast/GroupReduce with stream-level multi-stage overlap. FlashMask-3 uses NVSHMEM [NVIDIA, 2023] GPU-initiated one-sided communication with zerocopy symmetric buffers shared with the attention kernel, achieving high overlap without perturbing the WGMMA critical path. Mesh-Attention [Chen et al., 2025] reduces communication volume from O(N d) to O(N d/ ) via 2D assignment matrix, topological optimization orthogonal and composable with FlashMask-3s latency-focused NVSHMEM overlap.

For fixed set of weights the assignment is deterministic, so we compute it ahead of time and overlap it with the compute and communication of the previous iteration, and reuse it across layers through cache keyed on the mask pattern. The cost is not negligible in absolute terms, which is why it is prefetched rather than run inline.
